title: The Failing Glass Factory in Fujian That Nobody Dared Take Over
dek: In 1983 Cao Dewang took charge of a loss-making township factory that made water-meter glass, and two years later turned it to car windows.

story.company: Gao Shan Special Glass (later Fuyao Glass)
story.event: Taking over a loss-making township glass factory and turning it to car glass
story.summary: In 1983 Cao Dewang, who had worked since 1976 at the Gao Shan Special Glass Factory, a loss-making township enterprise in Fuqing, Fujian, that made glass for water meters, took charge of it and had it in profit within a year. In 1985 he moved it into car glass after finding imported glass sold at prices he called shameless, and in 1987 he founded Fuyao Glass, which grew into the world's largest automotive glass supplier.
paragraphs: In 1976 Cao Dewang went to work as a merchandiser for the Gao Shan Special Glass Factory, a small township enterprise in Fuqing, in Fujian province, that made glass for water meters. He had left school at 14 to herd oxen, and had traded tobacco leaves and fruit when private trade was banned. By 1983 the factory was losing money, and the local authority, by the account Ernst & Young gave in 2009, had no means of turning it round.

Cao took it on. The terms are told differently: Fuyao's own timeline says he contracted the factory, while the Financial Times reported that the local government agreed to sell it to him and that he paid with savings from his trading. The risk was political as much as commercial. "No one dared to take over the factory, as it was run by the Communist party," he said in 2014. Deng Xiaoping's reforms were a few years old, and, he said, nobody yet believed the party meant them; had the new rules not come after he took over, "I would have spent Chinese new year in prison." Within a year, the FT reported, the factory made a profit of Rmb200,000.

He kept making water-meter glass until 1985, when he learnt that Japanese companies were selling car glass in China for several thousand renminbi, a price he called "shameless". As he later described it, nobody in China made automotive glass, so repair shops had to import it; large firms did not want so small a business and small ones could not manage it. He moved the enterprise into car glass with the goal of "making affordable glass for the Chinese". The FT reported that he could make a panel for Rmb50 and sell it for Rmb1,500, well under the imports.

In 1987 he founded Fuyao Glass, which at the start was, he said, "really small, with only a million-level registered capital." Its first carmaker order, from Guangzhou Peugeot, came in 1989, and it listed in Shanghai in 1993. By the mid-2010s Fuyao described itself as the world's largest supplier of automotive glass. Cao said he had worked sixteen hours a day, every day of the year, for more than two decades.

quote.text: When he is angry, he thinks of the difficulties (his anger may involve him in). When he sees gain to be got, he thinks of righteousness.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Cao's anger at a "shameless" price set the course of his working life, and his own panels still sold at thirty times what they cost to make. Confucius asks two things of such a moment: count what the anger may cost you, and set righteousness beside the gain. The story answers the first more clearly than the second.

reflection: Cao's turn began with irritation: a price he thought indecent, and a gap that nobody nearby was filling. Irritation is useful information. It often points at work that needs doing, and you have probably felt it at a stock-out, a delayed result or an invoice that made no sense.

Confucius would let you keep the anger but ask for two more things: a plain look at what acting on it might cost you, and an honest answer about what you would charge if you held the advantage. Cao also said he worked sixteen hours a day for twenty years. That is one part of his story you do not have to carry with you.
invitation: Write down one price or delay in your working week that strikes you as unfair. Beside it, note what a fair version would cost and who would pay for it. Then leave the note alone for today.

cross_checks.claim: In 1983 Cao took charge of the loss-making Gao Shan glass factory, where he had worked since 1976, and had it in profit within a year.
The factory made glass for water meters.
In 1985 Cao moved the enterprise into automotive glass because car glass was imported and expensive.
Fuyao listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1993.
Fuyao became the world's largest automotive glass supplier.

research_notes: The slate dated this episode to 1987; the takeover was in 1983, the turn to car glass in 1985 and the founding of Fuyao in 1987, so the story runs 1983 to 1987. Terms of the takeover differ: Fuyao's own milestones page says Cao 'contracts' the Gaoshan factory (the usual Chinese term for leasing a collective enterprise under the 1980s responsibility system); the FT (2014) says the local government agreed to sell it to him and that he paid from trading savings; Ernst & Young (2009), Fuyao's 2016 award page and Glass International say he was asked or invited to take it over. The story gives the company's and the FT's versions side by side and does not choose. Product: the FT and Cao himself (LEADERS, 2015) say water-meter glass; Glass International calls it a flat-glass processing business; a 2013 Glass on Web interview, no longer online, reportedly said hydrometers. The story uses Cao's own description. Pivot year: the FT and Cao give 1985; a 2025 Caixin Global timeline (paywalled, not cited) gives 1986, and also dates the 'official' establishment of Fuyao Glass to 1995, against 1987 in Fuyao's own materials, the FT and Ernst & Young; the story uses 1985 and 1987. The Rmb200,000 first-year profit and the Rmb50 cost and Rmb1,500 price appear only in the FT, so they are attributed to it; Ernst & Young confirms only a profit within a year. The 16-hours-a-day figure is Cao's own claim. Ernst & Young places the founding in Fuzhou (the registered seat) while the factory was in Fuqing; the story does not name a founding city. Cao is also known by his Cantonese name, Cho Tak Wong, which Fuyao's English materials use. The FT article is cited from euro2day.gr's licensed republication because ft.com is paywalled. The Confucius line is one of nine things the superior man considers; it is applied to Cao's decision by analogy.
